cards.front: Which atmospheric layer is hidden?
cards.back: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere

cards.front: Put the layers in order from the ground up.
cards.back: Troposphere → Stratosphere → Mesosphere → Thermosphere → Exosphere

cards.front: Dry air is about {{78%}} nitrogen, {{21%}} oxygen and about 1% argon (CO₂ is only about 0.04%).
cards.back: N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%, Ar about 0.9%, CO₂ about 0.04%.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a pie chart of the air with three slices: nitrogen, oxygen and 'everything else'. Label the percentages.

cards.front: Which layer holds most of the air's mass and all the weather?
cards.back: The troposphere (0 to about 12 km). It holds about 75-80% of the air's mass. Temperature falls with height here.

cards.front: Why does the stratosphere get warmer with height?
cards.back: The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet (UV) light from the Sun and turns it into heat. Most ozone sits at about 20-30 km.

cards.front: Match each layer to how temperature changes with height.
cards.back: Troposphere = cools with height; Stratosphere = warms with height; Mesosphere = cools with height; Thermosphere = warms with height

cards.front: How high is the tropopause, and where is it highest?
cards.back: About 9 km over the poles and 17 km over the equator (average about 12 km). Warm tropical air rises higher.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the Earth from the pole to the equator and sketch the tropopause as a line that is low at the poles and high at the equator.

cards.front: Compare a cold front and a warm front: slope, speed and weather.
cards.back: Cold front: steep slope, fast, thunderstorms and showers, then cooler. Warm front: gentle slope, slow, wide steady rain, then warmer.

cards.front: Match each air mass code to its source and feel.
cards.back: cP = continental polar: cold and dry; mP = maritime polar: cool and moist; cT = continental tropical: hot and dry; mT = maritime tropical: warm and moist
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a world map and shade where each of the four air masses (cP, mP, cT, mT) forms.

cards.front: In the Northern Hemisphere, how does air move around a low-pressure center?
cards.back: Counterclockwise and inward, and it rises. Rising air makes clouds and rain.

cards.front: What weather goes with a high-pressure system and why?
cards.back: Clear, calm and dry. Air sinks and warms, so clouds evaporate. It spirals clockwise and outward (Northern Hemisphere).

cards.front: Order the life of a mid-latitude cyclone.
cards.back: Cold and warm air meet at a stationary front → A wave forms on the front → Warm and cold fronts develop around a low → The cold front catches the warm front (occlusion) → The cyclone weakens
items: Cold and warm air meet at a stationary front
A wave forms on the front
Warm and cold fronts develop around a low
The cold front catches the warm front (occlusion)

cards.front: A {{cold}} front moves faster than a warm front, so it can catch up with it and form an {{occluded}} front.
cards.back: Cold fronts move about 2 times faster than warm fronts.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a weather map of a low with a blue triangle line (cold front) chasing a red semicircle line (warm front).

cards.front: Which way does the Coriolis effect turn moving air in each hemisphere?
cards.back: To the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. It is zero at the equator.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the Earth from above the North Pole with an arrow going straight south. Draw how it curves to the right.

cards.front: Which part of the water cycle is hidden?
cards.back: Evaporation, Condensation, Precipitation, Runoff, Infiltration, Transpiration

cards.front: Relative humidity = {{actual water vapor}} ÷ {{maximum vapor at that temperature}} × 100%.
cards.back: RH tells how close the air is to saturation (100%).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a bucket with a fill line. Label the bucket 'maximum vapor at this temperature' and the water 'actual vapor'. Write RH = water ÷ bucket.

cards.front: What is the dew point?
cards.back: The temperature to which air must be cooled (at constant pressure) to become saturated, RH = 100%. Below it, dew or cloud droplets form.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a cold glass of lemonade with water drops on the outside. Mark the drops 'dew point reached'.

cards.front: If air warms but gains no vapor, what happens to relative humidity?
cards.back: It falls, because warm air can hold more vapor. Cool air at night: RH rises, fog may form.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two buckets: a small one labeled 'cool air' and a bigger one labeled 'warm air', both with the same water level.

cards.front: Order how a raindrop forms in a rising air parcel.
cards.back: Air rises and cools → Air reaches saturation → Vapor condenses on condensation nuclei → Droplets collide and grow → Drops become heavy and fall

cards.front: Match the precipitation type to its description.
cards.back: Drizzle = very small drops, under 0.5 mm; Sleet = frozen raindrops (ice pellets); Hail = layered ice balls from cumulonimbus; Snow = ice crystals falling
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four small pictures in a row: tiny dots (drizzle), small ice beads (sleet), a ball with onion layers (hail), a six-armed crystal (snow).

cards.front: Why are condensation nuclei needed for clouds?
cards.back: Water vapor needs a surface to condense on. Tiny particles like dust, sea salt and smoke act as nuclei for droplets.

cards.front: Which circulation cell is hidden?
cards.back: Hadley cell, Ferrel cell, Polar cell

cards.front: Match each wind belt to its latitude and direction.
cards.back: Trade winds = 0°-30°, blow from the east; Westerlies = 30°-60°, blow from the west; Polar easterlies = 60°-90°, blow from the east; Horse latitudes = about 30°, calm sinking air

cards.front: What is the Coriolis effect and where is it strongest?
cards.back: Earth's rotation seems to deflect moving air right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern. Zero at the equator, strongest at the poles.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a globe with an arrow from the equator to the North Pole. Show it bending east (right) because the Earth spins.

cards.front: What is the ITCZ?
cards.back: The Intertropical Convergence Zone, where the trade winds from both hemispheres meet near the equator. Air rises there, giving heavy rain. It shifts north and south with the seasons.

cards.front: Wind blows from {{high}} to {{low}} pressure, pushed by the {{pressure gradient}} force and then turned by the Coriolis effect.
cards.back: High to low pressure.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a hill (high pressure) and a valley (low pressure) with a ball rolling down. Label the ball 'wind'.

cards.front: What are jet streams?
cards.back: Fast, narrow rivers of air near the top of the troposphere (about 10 km), flowing west to east. They sit near cell boundaries (about 30° and 60°).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a side view of the troposphere with a thick arrow near the top labeled 'jet stream'. Mark the 30° and 60° boundaries on the ground.

cards.front: Which belts of surface pressure are low and which are high?
cards.back: Low: the equator (0°) and 60°. High: 30° and the poles (90°). Rising air means low pressure, sinking air means high.

cards.front: Which cloud type is hidden?
cards.back: Cirrus, Altocumulus, Stratus, Nimbostratus, Cumulonimbus

cards.front: Which part of the hurricane is hidden?
cards.back: Eye, Eyewall, Rainbands

cards.front: What happens in El Niño and La Niña?
cards.back: El Niño: trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, Peru gets rain and Indonesia drought. La Niña: stronger trade winds, cooler eastern Pacific.

cards.front: What causes a monsoon?
cards.back: Land heats and cools faster than the ocean, so winds reverse by season. Summer: wet winds from the sea. Winter: dry winds from the land.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two panels: summer (sea → hot land, with rain clouds) and winter (cold land → sea, dry). Add arrows for the wind.

cards.front: When do sea breezes and land breezes blow?
cards.back: Sea breeze: day, wind blows from the cooler sea to the warmer land. Land breeze: night, from the cooler land to the warmer sea.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a beach in daytime with an arrow from the sea to land, then at night with the arrow reversed.

cards.front: Order the life of an ordinary thunderstorm cell.
cards.back: Cumulus stage: updraft only → Mature stage: updraft and downdraft, heavy rain → Dissipating stage: downdraft only
items: Mature stage: updraft and downdraft, heavy rain

cards.front: Match the name to the region.
cards.back: Same storm, different names. Winds of 119 km/h (74 mph) or more make it a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a world map and mark where hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones occur.

cards.front: Which river feature is hidden?
cards.back: Cut bank, Point bar, Oxbow lake

cards.front: River discharge Q = {{cross-section area}} × {{velocity}}, measured in {{m³/s}}.
cards.back: Q = A × v = width × depth × velocity.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a river cross-section as a rectangle. Label width w and depth d. Write A = w × d and Q = A × v.

cards.front: A river is 10 m wide and 2 m deep and flows at 1.5 m/s. What is its discharge?
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the river cross-section with 10 m and 2 m labeled, then an arrow for the 1.5 m/s flow.

cards.front: How does a delta form?
cards.back: A river slows down when it enters a lake or the sea, so it drops its sediment. The sediment builds up a fan-shaped delta.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a river flowing into the sea with a triangle of sediment at its mouth and a few branching channels.

cards.front: Match the river feature to how it forms.
cards.back: V-shaped valley = downcutting by a fast river; Waterfall = hard rock over soft rock; Floodplain = deposits when the river floods; Levee = ridge of sediment next to the channel
pairs: ridge of sediment next to the channel
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a river cross-section on a floodplain. Mark the levee on each bank.

cards.front: Order a river from source to sea.
cards.back: Upper course: steep, V-shaped valley → Middle course: meanders → Lower course: wide floodplain → Mouth: delta
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the long profile of a river: a steep curve at the start that gets gentler. Label the four parts.

cards.front: What happens to particles when river speed drops?
cards.back: The river can no longer carry the largest particles, so they are dropped first (boulders, gravel, then sand, then silt and clay). Fast water carries and erodes more.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a river slowing down with big pebbles dropped first, then sand, then fine mud further along.

cards.front: Which part of the ocean conveyor belt is hidden?
cards.back: Deep water formation, Upwelling

cards.front: Which part of the wave is hidden?
cards.back: Crest, Trough, Wavelength, Wave height

cards.front: What is the average salinity of seawater, and where is it highest and lowest?
cards.back: About 35 g of salt per kg (35 ‰). Highest in dry subtropics where evaporation beats rain. Lowest near river mouths and in rainy or melting areas.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a graph with latitude on the x-axis and salinity on the y-axis. Make a dip at the equator, peaks at 20-30°, dips at the poles.

cards.front: What are the thermocline, halocline and pycnocline?
cards.back: Layers where temperature, salinity or density change quickly with depth. The pycnocline separates light surface water from dense deep water and stops mixing.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a vertical profile of the ocean: warm at the top, a steep drop in temperature (thermocline), then cold deep water.

cards.front: What drives surface currents, and what are gyres?
cards.back: Winds and the Coriolis effect. Big circular currents called gyres turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern. The Gulf Stream is a warm current.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the North Atlantic: a clockwise loop with the warm Gulf Stream on the west side going north.

cards.front: What is the difference between spring tides and neap tides?
cards.back: Spring tides (largest range) at new and full moon, when Sun, Earth and Moon line up. Neap tides (smallest range) at the quarter moons, at right angles.

cards.front: What causes a tsunami and how fast does it travel?
cards.back: Sudden movement of the sea floor (quake, landslide, volcano). Speed v = √(g × depth): about 200 m/s over 4 km. It slows and grows taller near the coast.

cards.front: Match the ocean sediment to its source.
cards.back: Terrigenous = from land: sand, mud; Biogenous = shells and skeletons (ooze); Hydrogenous = precipitates from seawater (nodules); Cosmogenous = dust and meteorites from space
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw an ocean floor profile and mark where each of the four sediment types would be found.

cards.front: What is longshore drift?
cards.back: Waves hit the beach at an angle and push sand up the beach (swash). The backwash runs straight down. Sand moves in a zigzag along the coast.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a beach from above. Show waves arriving at an angle and the zigzag path of a sand grain.

cards.front: Which part of the glacier is hidden?
cards.back: Accumulation zone, Ablation zone, Equilibrium line, Terminal moraine

cards.front: Which valley shape is hidden?
cards.back: V-shaped valley, U-shaped valley

cards.front: How does a glacier form?
cards.back: Snow piles up faster than it melts. Buried snow turns into granular firn, then into dense glacial ice (about 0.9 g/cm³) under pressure over years. The ice then flows downhill.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw 3 stages in a row: fluffy snow, rounded firn grains, solid blue ice. Add arrows for time and pressure.

cards.front: Match the glacial landform to its description.
cards.back: Cirque = bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a glacier; Arête = sharp ridge between two cirques; Horn = pyramid-shaped peak; Fjord = glacial valley flooded by the sea
pairs: bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a glacier
glacial valley flooded by the sea
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a mountain with three cirques around it. Mark the horn in the middle and the arêtes between the cirques.

cards.front: Mass balance = accumulation − {{ablation}}. If it is positive the glacier {{advances}}; if negative it retreats.
cards.back: Snow gain minus melt and ice loss per year.

cards.front: What are till, moraines and erratics?
cards.back: Till is unsorted rock debris dropped by ice. Moraines are ridges of till (lateral, medial, terminal). Erratics are large boulders carried far from their source rock.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a glacier from above with lateral moraines at the sides, a medial moraine in the middle and a terminal moraine at the front.

cards.front: What are a drumlin, an esker and a kettle?
cards.back: Drumlin: streamlined hill of till shaped along ice flow. Esker: winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel from a stream under the ice. Kettle: hollow (often a lake) left by a melted ice block.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a plan view with an oval drumlin, a snaking esker line and a round kettle lake.

cards.front: Which part of the groundwater system is hidden?
cards.back: Unsaturated zone, Water table, Aquifer, Aquitard

cards.front: Porosity = {{volume of pores}} ÷ {{total volume}}. Permeability is how easily water flows through {{connected}} pores.
cards.back: Porosity tells how much water a rock can hold; permeability how fast it can flow.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a box of rock with dots as pores. Show connected pores with lines (permeable) and isolated pores (not).

cards.front: Clay has high porosity but is a poor aquifer. Why?
cards.back: Its pores are tiny and poorly connected, so water cannot flow through (low permeability). It makes a good aquitard.

cards.front: Match each material to its porosity and permeability.
cards.back: Gravel = high porosity, high permeability; Clay = high porosity, very low permeability; Sandstone = medium porosity, medium permeability; Unfractured granite = very low porosity and permeability
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw four boxes showing big round grains (gravel), tiny flat grains (clay), cemented grains (sandstone) and solid crystals (granite).

cards.front: What is an artesian well?
cards.back: A well in a confined aquifer, trapped between aquitards. Water pressure from higher ground pushes the water up, sometimes to the surface without a pump.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a tilted aquifer between two clay layers with a well. Show the water level rising above the aquifer in the pipe.

cards.front: What is a cone of depression?
cards.back: A funnel-shaped dip in the water table around a well that is pumping. Over-pumping makes it deeper and can dry shallow wells nearby.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a well with the water table curving down toward it like a funnel.

cards.front: Where does a spring appear?
cards.back: Where the water table meets the land surface, often on a hillside or at the edge of an aquitard.

cards.front: Which mineral in Bowen's series is hidden?
cards.back: Olivine, Pyroxene, Amphibole, Biotite, Quartz

cards.front: Order the Mohs scale from softest (1) to hardest (10).
cards.back: Talc → Gypsum → Calcite → Fluorite → Apatite → Orthoclase feldspar → Quartz → Topaz → Corundum → Diamond

cards.front: Order the discontinuous branch of Bowen's series from first to crystallize.
cards.back: Olivine → Pyroxene → Amphibole → Biotite

cards.front: What does a phase diagram show?
cards.back: Which phase (solid, liquid, gas) is stable for each temperature and pressure. Lines are boundaries. At the triple point all three phases coexist.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a pressure (y) versus temperature (x) graph for water with solid, liquid and gas regions and the triple point.

cards.front: Match the mineral property to its meaning.
cards.back: Luster = how the surface reflects light; Streak = color of the powder; Cleavage = breaks along flat planes; Fracture = breaks in an irregular way
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a mineral with flat shiny faces (cleavage) next to one with a curved, shell-like break (conchoidal fracture).

cards.front: What is a mineral?
cards.back: A naturally occurring, inorganic, solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure. Coal is not a mineral (organic). Ice is.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a crystal of quartz and write the four rules of what makes a mineral beside it.

cards.front: Calcite has hardness {{3}} and {{fizzes}} in dilute acid; quartz has hardness {{7}}.
cards.back: Quick tests: scratch test and acid test.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a calcite crystal with a drop of acid and bubbles on it.

cards.front: Which part of the rock cycle is hidden?
cards.back: Magma, Igneous, Sediment, Sedimentary, Metamorphic

cards.front: Which igneous body is hidden?
cards.back: Dike, Sill, Laccolith, Batholith

cards.front: Match the rock to its type.
cards.back: Granite = intrusive igneous; Basalt = extrusive igneous; Limestone = sedimentary; Marble = metamorphic

cards.front: How does silica content change magma behavior?
cards.back: More silica (felsic, over 63% SiO₂): light color, thick (viscous), explosive, low temperature. Less silica (mafic, 45-52%): dark, runny, gentle eruptions. Rhyolite is felsic and basalt is mafic.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two volcanoes: a wide gentle one with runny lava (basalt) and a steep one with an explosive ash cloud (rhyolite/andesite).

cards.front: How does cooling speed change igneous crystal size?
cards.back: Slow cooling underground gives large crystals (granite, gabbro). Fast cooling at the surface gives tiny crystals or glass (basalt, obsidian).

cards.front: What are the two main kinds of metamorphism, and what is foliation?
cards.back: Contact: heat from nearby magma. Regional: heat and pressure during mountain building. Foliation is layering of minerals under pressure (slate, schist, gneiss). Marble and quartzite are non-foliated.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a magma body baking the rock around it (contact) and a mountain belt squeezing rock (regional).

cards.front: Order shale by increasing metamorphic grade.
cards.back: Shale → Slate → Phyllite → Schist → Gneiss
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a ladder with 5 rungs from shale at the bottom to gneiss at the top. Add arrows for more heat and pressure.

cards.front: What do shield volcanoes and stratovolcanoes look like and erupt?
cards.back: Shield: broad and gentle, runny basalt (Hawaii). Stratovolcano: steep cone with layers of ash and lava, viscous andesite, explosive (Mount Merapi, Mount Fuji).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the outline of a shield volcano next to a steep stratovolcano and label the magma type.

cards.front: What do cross-bedding, ripple marks and mud cracks tell about the environment?
cards.back: Cross-bedding: moving water or wind (dunes, rivers). Ripple marks: shallow flowing water. Mud cracks: mud that dried in the air. Graded bedding: a sediment-filled flow settling.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three small rock faces: slanted layers (cross-bedding), a wavy top (ripples) and polygon cracks (mud cracks).

cards.front: Which layer of the Earth is hidden?
cards.back: Crust, Mantle, Outer core, Inner core

cards.front: Which type of plate boundary is hidden?
cards.back: Divergent, Convergent, Transform

cards.front: Which type of fault is hidden?
cards.back: Normal fault, Reverse fault, Strike-slip fault

cards.front: Which soil layer is hidden?
cards.back: Humus / litter, Topsoil, Subsoil, Weathered rock, Bedrock

cards.front: Match each layer to its state.
cards.back: Crust: solid, 5-70 km thick. Mantle: solid, flows slowly (to 2900 km). Outer core: liquid. Inner core: solid.

cards.front: Compare P waves and S waves.
cards.back: P: compressional, fastest, travel through solids, liquids and gases. S: shear (sideways), slower, only through solids. P arrives first.

cards.front: What are the P and S shadow zones and what do they prove?
cards.back: P waves are bent by the core: a shadow zone at 104°-140° from the quake. S waves stop at the liquid outer core: none beyond 104°. This showed the outer core is liquid.

cards.front: Match the place to its plate setting.
cards.back: Mid-Atlantic Ridge = divergent boundary; Andes mountains = ocean-continent subduction; Himalayas = continent-continent collision; San Andreas Fault = transform boundary
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a world map outline and mark each place with a different symbol for its boundary type.

cards.front: The longer the gap between the P-wave and S-wave arrivals, the {{farther}} the earthquake. P waves are {{faster}} than S waves.
cards.back: The S-P time gap gives the distance to the earthquake.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a seismogram with a small P wave first and a bigger S wave later. Mark the S-P gap with a double arrow.

cards.front: What drives plate tectonics?
cards.back: Heat in the mantle moves rock in slow convection. Plates move by slab pull (heavy sinking edge pulls the plate), ridge push and mantle drag, a few cm per year.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the mantle as a pot of soup with convection loops. Add two plates on top with arrows showing where they move.

cards.front: Which feature of the rock layers is hidden?
cards.back: Angular unconformity, Dike

cards.front: After each half-life, {{half}} of the parent atoms remain: N = N₀ × (½){{ⁿ}}, with n = time ÷ half-life.
cards.back: After 1, 2, 3 half-lives: 50%, 25%, 12.5%.

cards.front: State the four rules of relative dating.
cards.back: Superposition: older layers lie below. Original horizontality: layers form flat. Cross-cutting: a feature that cuts is younger. Inclusions: pieces inside are older than the rock around them.

cards.front: Match the unconformity to its description.
cards.back: Angular unconformity = tilted layers below horizontal layers; Disconformity = gap between parallel layers; Nonconformity = sediment on igneous or metamorphic rock
pairs: sediment on igneous or metamorphic rock

cards.front: Which isotopes are used for dating, and what are their half-lives?
cards.back: Carbon-14: 5730 years (up to about 50 000 years). Potassium-40: 1.25 billion years. Uranium-238 → lead-206: 4.47 billion years.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a number line from 5730 years to billions of years. Mark C-14, K-40 and U-238 on it.

cards.front: What is an index fossil?
cards.back: A fossil from a species that lived for a short time but spread widely. Finding the same one in two places shows those rock layers have the same age.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two rock columns far apart. Join the layers that hold the same ammonite fossil with a line.

cards.front: How do you read strike and dip on a geologic map?
cards.back: Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on a tilted layer. Dip is the angle it slopes down and the direction it slopes. The short tick of the symbol points down-dip with the angle written next to it.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a tilted layer. Mark the strike line, the dip arrow and the symbol with '30' next to it.

cards.front: Which point of the orbit is hidden?
cards.back: Perihelion, Aphelion

cards.front: Kepler's third law: T² = {{a³}} when T is in years and a is in {{AU}}.
cards.back: T² ∝ a³ for all planets around the Sun.

cards.front: State Kepler's second law and what it says about speed.
cards.back: A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. So a planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion.

cards.front: Newton's gravity: F = {{G M m / r²}}. If the distance doubles, the force becomes {{one quarter}}.
cards.back: Inverse-square law.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two circles (masses) with arrows between them. Show the distance r. Then draw twice the distance with a quarter-size arrow.

cards.front: How do two stars in a binary system orbit?
cards.back: Both orbit the common center of mass (barycenter). The heavier star is closer to it and moves slower. For binaries: M₁ + M₂ = a³ ÷ T² (solar masses, AU, years).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two stars of different sizes orbiting a common point, with the big star on a small circle and the small star on a big circle.

cards.front: What are the Doppler formula and the colors of its shifts?
cards.back: Δλ / λ = v / c. Moving away: longer wavelength, redshift. Moving closer: shorter wavelength, blueshift.

cards.front: Name three kinds of binary star by how we detect them.
cards.back: Visual binary: both seen separately. Eclipsing binary: brightness dips as they pass in front. Spectroscopic binary: spectral lines shift back and forth (Doppler).
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a light curve with two dips of different depth for an eclipsing binary.

cards.front: When is Earth at perihelion and aphelion, and what causes the seasons?
cards.back: Perihelion about 3 January (0.983 AU), aphelion about 4 July (1.017 AU). Seasons come from the 23.4° tilt of Earth's axis, not from distance.

cards.front: State Wien's law and what it says about star colors.
cards.back: λmax × T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K. Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths: hot stars look blue-white, cool stars look red.

cards.front: Stefan–Boltzmann law: L = {{4πR²σT⁴}}. Doubling the temperature makes a star {{16}} times more luminous.
cards.back: Power grows with the fourth power of T.

cards.front: What is albedo and what are typical values?
cards.back: Albedo is the fraction of sunlight reflected, from 0 to 1. Fresh snow about 0.8, Earth average about 0.3, forest about 0.12, ocean about 0.06.

cards.front: What is the inverse-square law for light?
cards.back: Flux F = L ÷ (4πd²). Doubling the distance spreads the same light over 4 times the area, so the flux falls to a quarter.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a star with light going through a small square at distance d and a square 4 times larger at 2d.

cards.front: How does the magnitude scale work?
cards.back: Smaller (or more negative) means brighter. 5 magnitudes = 100 times brighter, so 1 magnitude ≈ 2.512 times. Sun -26.7, Sirius -1.46, naked-eye limit about +6.

cards.front: Match the star to its surface temperature and color.
cards.back: Sun = about 5800 K, yellow-white; Sirius A = about 9900 K, blue-white; Betelgeuse = about 3500 K, red; Rigel = about 12 000 K, blue-white

cards.front: What are absolute magnitude and the distance modulus?
cards.back: Absolute magnitude M is the magnitude a star would have at 10 parsecs. Distance modulus: m − M = 5 log₁₀(d ÷ 10 pc).

cards.front: Which part of the celestial sphere is hidden?
cards.back: North celestial pole, Vernal equinox, Celestial equator, Ecliptic

cards.front: Which part of the northern sky is hidden?
cards.back: Polaris, Pointer stars, Big Dipper, Cassiopeia

cards.front: Which part of Orion is hidden?
cards.back: Betelgeuse, Rigel, Belt, M42

cards.front: Match each star to its facts.
cards.back: Sirius = α CMa, brightest star in the night sky; Betelgeuse = α Ori, red supergiant; Rigel = β Ori, blue-white supergiant; Vega = α Lyr, bright star in Lyra; Polaris = α UMi, the north star; Proxima Centauri = α Cen C, the nearest star
pairs: α CMa, brightest star in the night sky
α Lyr, bright star in Lyra
α Cen C, the nearest star

cards.front: Match each deep-sky object to its name.
cards.back: M42 = Orion Nebula; M31 = Andromeda Galaxy; M1 = Crab Nebula (supernova remnant); M45 = Pleiades open cluster

cards.front: Order the zodiac constellations as the Sun passes through them, starting with Aries.
cards.back: Aries → Taurus → Gemini → Cancer → Leo → Virgo → Libra → Scorpius → Sagittarius → Capricornus → Aquarius → Pisces
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a circle (the ecliptic) and place the 12 constellation names around it.

cards.front: Match the zodiac constellation to its IAU abbreviation.
cards.back: Cancer = Cnc; Scorpius = Sco; Sagittarius = Sgr; Capricornus = Cap; Aquarius = Aqr; Pisces = Psc

cards.front: What is a circumpolar star?
cards.back: A star that never sets for an observer. For northern latitude φ, a star is circumpolar if its declination is greater than 90° − φ. Polaris's altitude equals the observer's latitude.

cards.front: When are the equinoxes and solstices, and where is the Sun then?
cards.back: Mar equinox (~20 Mar) and Sep equinox (~23 Sep): Sun on the celestial equator, dec 0°. June solstice (~21 Jun): dec +23.4°. Dec solstice (~21 Dec): dec −23.4°.

cards.front: How does stellar parallax give a distance?
cards.back: As Earth orbits, a nearby star shifts against distant stars. d (parsecs) = 1 ÷ p (arcseconds). Proxima Centauri has p = 0.77″, so d ≈ 1.30 pc ≈ 4.2 light-years.

cards.front: Match the constellation to a feature that helps you find it.
cards.back: Orion = belt of three stars; Ursa Major = the Big Dipper; Ursa Minor = contains Polaris; Cassiopeia = W or M shape; Lyra = bright star Vega; Andromeda = contains the M31 galaxy
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw the shapes of Orion, the Big Dipper and Cassiopeia as simple dot-to-dot patterns.

cards.front: Which phase of the Moon is hidden?
cards.back: New Moon, Waxing crescent, First quarter, Waxing gibbous, Full Moon, Waning gibbous, Third quarter, Waning crescent

cards.front: Which part of the shadow is hidden?
cards.back: Penumbra, Umbra

cards.front: Which part of the Solar System is hidden?
cards.back: Asteroid belt, Kuiper belt

cards.front: Order the planets from the Sun.
cards.back: Mercury → Venus → Earth → Mars → Jupiter → Saturn → Uranus → Neptune

cards.front: The Moon orbits Earth in {{27.3}} days (sidereal) but its phases repeat every {{29.5}} days (synodic).
cards.back: Earth also moves around the Sun, so the Moon needs about 2 more days to return to the same phase.

cards.front: Why is there no eclipse every month?
cards.back: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's orbit. Most months the Moon passes above or below the Sun-Earth line. Eclipses need a new or full moon near a node.

cards.front: Match each space mission to what it did.
cards.back: Apollo 11 = first crewed Moon landing, 1969; Voyager 2 = flew past all four giant planets; Cassini = orbited Saturn, 2004-2017; New Horizons = Pluto flyby, 2015; Perseverance = Mars rover, landed 2021
pairs: flew past all four giant planets
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a line through the Solar System and mark each mission where it went.

cards.front: Give key facts about the Earth-Moon system.
cards.back: Distance about 384 400 km (light takes 1.3 s). The Moon always shows the same face (synchronous rotation). It is slowly moving away, about 3.8 cm per year.
